data.title: The Strong Earnings Posted By Mansei (TSE:7565) Are A Good Indication Of The Strength Of The Business
data.description:

A Closer Look At Mansei's Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. You could think of the accrual ratio from cashflow as the 'non-FCF profit ratio'.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

Mansei has an accrual ratio of -0.34 for the year to September 2026. That indicates that its free cash flow quite significantly exceeded its statutory profit. Indeed, in the last twelve months it reported free cash flow of JP¥3.2b, well over the JP¥1.32b it reported in profit. Zooming In On China Aviation Oil (Singapore)'s Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

Therefore, it's actually considered a good thing when a company has a negative accrual ratio, but a bad thing if its accrual ratio is positive. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

For the year to September 2026, China Aviation Oil (Singapore) had an accrual ratio of 0.48. As a general rule, that bodes poorly for future profitability. To wit, the company did not generate one whit of free cashflow in that time. Over the last year it actually had negative free cash flow of US$187m, in contrast to the aforementioned profit of US$82.8m. It's worth noting that China Aviation Oil (Singapore) generated positive FCF of US$144m a year ago, so at least they've done it in the past. The good news for shareholders is that China Aviation Oil (Singapore)'s accrual ratio was much better last year, so this year's poor reading might simply be a case of a short term mismatch between profit and FCF. As a result, some shareholders may be looking for stronger cash conversion in the current year.

Does Hang Pin Living Technology Have A Long Cash Runway?

A company's cash runway is the amount of time it would take to burn through its cash reserves at its current cash burn rate. In September 2026, Hang Pin Living Technology had HK$91m in cash, and was debt-free. Importantly, its cash burn was HK$43m over the trailing twelve months. How Easily Can Hang Pin Living Technology Raise Cash?

data.description:
Anthropic’s record-breaking US$81b IPO has thrown a spotlight on capital markets, with a US$2t valuation putting AI enthusiasm front and centre for deal makers. When money flows at that scale, the banks and brokers that arrange, underwrite, and distribute offerings can see their pipelines reshape quickly. This piece walks through 3 financial stocks closely exposed to that AI IPO wave, showing where enthusiasm may help and where risks could lurk.

TPG (TPG)

TPG gives you pure-play exposure to alternative assets that intersect with equity capital markets, since its funds often rely on IPOs and other listings to cash out winners. The bullish analyst narrative on Simply Wall St frames that link in a very optimistic way.

TPG runs a global alternative asset platform, managing private equity, credit, real estate, and other investment vehicles that are closely tied to equity capital markets exit activity. Brokerage operations generated about US$4.6b of revenue, and the business carries a market value near US$17.9b.

"TPG is positioned to capitalize on the rising global demand for alternative investments, as seen by its record fundraising momentum, inflows from both institutional and private wealth channels, and expanding suite of strategies across private equity, credit, real estate, and infrastructure. This is expected to translate into sustained growth in assets under management and recurring management fees, potentially supporting higher revenue and fee-related earnings in coming years."

What really moves the needle for TPG now is how one emerging source of deal flow interacts with that fee engine over the next few years.

To see how that potential fee engine could accelerate or stall, read the full narrative for TPG and see what the IPO cycle may really mean for TPG.

EQT (OM:EQT)

EQT plugs directly into the Global Investment Banks and Capital Markets Franchises theme through its role as a listed private markets giant that depends on healthy equity markets for exits and fresh capital, and the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St argues that its AI oriented platform is built with that in mind.

"The build out of AI infrastructure and data center exposure, evidenced by the AI Infrastructure Fund reaching a net asset value of $11.5b and the rapid capacity expansion at EdgeConneX, positions EQT to capture additional management and performance fee income linked to AI related capital demand."

What happens to those fee streams if one key pressure on AI related capital demand shifts direction will be crucial for EQT holders.

If that pressure on AI capital starts to accelerate again, the full narrative for EQT shows how EQT’s fee engine could scale while some risks stay hidden in plain sight.

Partners Group Holding (SWX:PGHN)

Partners Group Holding sits in this capital markets screener as a large, listed private markets investor whose exits often rely on healthy IPO and equity issuance windows. It runs funds across private equity, infrastructure, real estate, credit and royalties, generating most revenue from private equity (CHF1.34b), infrastructure (CHF634m), private credit (CHF259m) and real estate (CHF226m), with a smaller royalties stream. Its market value is roughly CHF16.4b.

Partners Group Holding is one of the purest ways to access private markets through a listed stock. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St argues that its fundraising engine and product shelf with banks and wealth managers are central to that appeal.
